'''Riverbank Acoustical Laboratories (RAL)''', (often referred to as '''Riverbank''' or '''Riverbank Labs)''', is a [[NVLAP]] accredited acoustical testing agency founded by [[George Fabyan]] in 1913.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://riverbanklabs.com/about/|title=Riverbank Laboratories {{!}} About|language=en-US|access-date=2020-04-14}}</ref>{{Third-party inline|date=May 2020}}

The testing service remains a highly respected source of independent acoustical materials testing.  RAL specializes in STC ([[Sound transmission class|Sound Transmission Loss]] per ASTM E90), NRC ([[Sound absorption|Sound Absorption]] per ASTM C423), IIC ([[Impact insulation class|Impact Sound Transmission]] per ASTM E492), and [[Sound power|Sound Power]] (ISO 6926) testing. The current address for the company is 627 Riverbank Dr. Geneva, IL. This location also houses the Riverbank Acoustical Museum and Acoustical Library.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://riverbank.alionscience.com/ |title= Riverbank Labs website}}</ref><ref name=":0">{{cite book |last1=Fagone |first1=Jason |title=The Woman Who Smashed Codes |date=2017 |publisher=HarperCollins Publishers |isbn=978-0-06-243048-9}}</ref>

==History==

The acoustical laboratory building was funded and built by Colonel [[George Fabyan]] on his vast [[Fabyan Villa|Riverbank Estate]] in Geneva, Illinois.<ref name="Geneva1999">{{cite web |url=http://www.geneva.il.us/riverbnk/riverpag.htm |title=Riverbank History |date=1 February 1999 |author=Staff writer |website=City of Geneva, Illinois |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090727114137/http://www.geneva.il.us/riverbnk/riverpag.htm |archive-date=27 July 2009 |url-status=dead}}</ref>  Colonel Fabyan was a patron of obscure sciences, and references to his "Riverbank laboratories" exist as early as 1916.<ref>{{cite news |author=Staff Writer |date=17 April 1916 |title=Backs Cure for Cancer |url=https://www.newspapers.com/image/126911597/ |newspaper=The DeKalb Daily Chronicle |volume=18 |issue=120 |page=7 |location=DeKalb, Illinois |via=[[Newspapers.com]]}}</ref> In 1913, Fabyan hired [[Wallace Clement Sabine]] to help tune an acoustical levitation machine built according to specifications decoded from a Sir [[Francis Bacon]] work. Sabine ultimately convinced the colonel that the machine would never work, and the two became close friends. After hearing Sabine's complaints of the poor conditions of his acoustical test lab at Harvard, Colonel Fabyan agreed to build a state of the art reverberation chamber and test facility for Sabine to use on the property.

Sabine died in 1919, shortly after the lab was constructed. The task of managing the Laboratory Operations was granted to his cousin, [[Paul Sabine]], who refined the test methods and developed the lab into a successful business. After Paul retired, the lab operations were handed to Hale Sabine and the Armour Research Foundation of the Illinois Institute of Technology. The [[IIT Research Institute|Armour Research Foundation]] (ARF) was renamed [[IIT Research Institute|IITRI]] in 1963. IITRI funded a large expansion to the laboratory in the 1960s, which included a new [[transmission loss]] facility. In 2002, the technology and engineering divisions of IITRI (Including Riverbank Acoustical Laboratories) were spun off into a new company named Alion Science and Technology. Today, Alion conducts advanced acoustical testing operations in the facility for many prominent acoustical material manufacturers and government agencies.

In the facility's early days, it also housed a cryptology team that worked to decipher codes from the works of Sir Francis Bacon, Shakespeare, and enemy military communications.<ref name="Geneva1999"/> Fabyan allowed the U.S. Government to use Riverbank Laboratories to their disposal during World War I<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.nasaa-home.org/history/schools.htm |title=Intelligence Schools History |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20101206094837/http://nasaa-home.org/history/schools.htm |archivedate=2010-12-06 }}</ref> and German and Mexican codes were deciphered there. Much of the cryptanalysis was done by [[William F. Friedman|William]] and [[Elizebeth Smith Friedman|Elizebeth Friedman]].<ref name=":0" /> In 1993, the [[National Security Agency]] (NSA) recognized the work with a plaque reading  "To the Memory of George Fabyan From a Grateful Government: In recognition of the voluntary and confidential service rendered by Colonel Fabyan and his Riverbank Laboratories in the sensitive areas of [[cryptanalysis]] and cryptologic training during a critical time of national need on the eve of America's entry into World War I."<ref name="Rosenheim1997">{{cite book|author=Shawn Rosenheim|title=The Cryptographic Imagination: Secret Writing from Edgar Allan Poe to the Internet|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=sjhbAAAAMAAJ&pg=PA236|year=1997|publisher=Johns Hopkins University Press|isbn=978-0-8018-5331-9|page=236}}</ref><ref name="Laukaitis2004">{{cite book|last=Laukaitis|first=John J. |title=Geneva in Vintage Postcards|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=CbV9WRg_QRAC&pg=PA66|year=2004|publisher=Arcadia Publishing|isbn=978-0-7385-3347-6|page=66}}</ref> The building is recognized in the [[National Register of Historic Places]].<ref name="nris">{{NRISref|2013a|dateform=dmy|accessdate=October 17, 2017|refnum=03001204|name=Riverbank Laboratories}}</ref>
